A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same function-encoder work. Their main texts, equations, figures, and Appendices A–I are readable and support comparison despite pagination and figure-number changes.

before.justification: Section 4 reports original experiments on polynomial regression, CIFAR-100, 7-Scenes, and MuJoCo Ant. The appendices include original architecture and sensitivity analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds training-time measurements versus basis-function count in Appendix G, Figure 10.

M1.justification: The coefficient calculation, training objective, inference procedure, and architectures are unchanged. Appendix A's newly displayed regularizer repeats the formula already present in v1's Algorithm 1.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same four datasets and transfer scenarios. The new timing analysis uses these existing datasets; discussion of disjoint input distributions adds no evaluated scenario.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain FE (IP), autoencoders, transformers, TFE, the oracle, BF, BFB, MAML, and the CIFAR-specific Siamese and prototypical networks. The added Siamese discussion introduces no new comparator.

E3.justification: The added timing analysis measures percentage training-time increase relative to one basis function while varying the basis count through 100 across all four datasets. Existing predictive evaluation settings, splits, preprocessing, and model budgets remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix G adds a computational-cost analysis of increasing basis count, complementing the existing predictive-performance sweep. Architecture comparisons, example-count ablations, and the cross-entropy analysis are retained.

E5.justification: Existing ablations retain three seeds per setting, averaging over the last 50 evaluations, and minimum/median/maximum reporting. v2 introduces no revised run-count statement or new uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: New Figure 10 reports less than 20% additional training time for up to 100 basis functions relative to one across the four datasets. All previously included empirical plot images, including appendix results, are unchanged.

T1.justification: The formal transfer definitions, assumptions, approximation theorem, full proof, and inner-product derivations are retained. Changing the convex-hull notation and redisplaying the existing regularizer do not alter the mathematics.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion retain the same claims concerning three transfer types, least-squares function encoders, universal approximation, and performance on four benchmarks.

C2.justification: Appendix I adds a tentative explanation of Siamese performance through mean embeddings and maximum mean discrepancy. Appendix D explicitly discusses disjoint input distributions, while Appendix G interprets the timing results as supporting generous basis-count choices.

D1.justification: Appendix G adds relative training-cost information and practical guidance to overestimate the function-space dimensionality when choosing the basis count, suggesting 100 suffices for many problems. This is additional guidance, not evidence of changed existing implementations.

R1.justification: The cited works and main related-work discussion remain unchanged. The new Appendix I paragraph adds a limited conceptual connection between Siamese networks, the paper's basis-function perspective, and kernel mean embeddings.

P1.justification: v2 makes localized wording and notation edits, adds affiliations and acknowledgments, and expands several appendix explanations. The main narrative and appendix organization remain substantially unchanged.

P2.justification: v2 adds the four-panel training-time Figure 10 and redisplays the regularization equation. Existing figures retain their visual content but undergo some relocation and renumbering, alongside front-matter and page-layout adjustments.

improvement.justification: v1 examined how basis count affects predictive performance; v2 adds computational-cost evidence and concrete selection guidance, making that tradeoff more useful to readers. The regularization clarification and qualified explanatory discussion modestly improve exposition. The central method, theoretical support, and existing benchmark evidence remain unchanged.
